Today we discuss the idea of civilization and first I want to present to you the general understanding of how we get civilization and then I will present an alternative. So the traditional understanding is the Marxist understanding: this idea proposed by Karl Marx and it's the dominant one. In the beginning, we were hunter-gatherers and it sucked because you couldn't find food. Then we discovered agriculture, farming that allowed for surplus food—surplus just means that you have more food than you can eat—and so now you have people who don't have to work.

An elite arises from this surplus. And as such, they can engage in activities that improve the well-being of everyone and which create the basis for civilization. These things include religion—just myths and stories—but also arts, dance, music, paintings, and then of course you have science and technology. With these three things in place, now you can grow as a society. You can build cities because now you can have irrigation and farming. You can direct the river flow so you can use more farmland. And then you can have a hereditary elite who can focus their entire time on innovation, science, and progress.

Okay? Then you have writing because only a hereditarily privileged elite has the time and resources to learn how to write. Remember back then, writing was a very difficult activity; you had to spend your entire life learning it and practicing it. And together with this, you have the idea of money and property. These four things are what we refer to as civilization. Now there are good things that come from civilization: religion, arts, and science. But there are also bad things, which include war, slavery, and debt.

Today I wanted to propose an alternative, and I think this is a much more compelling one. The idea is that very from the very beginning we were religious, artistic, and capable of science. We do not need an elite to do this for us; we are all capable of doing it by ourselves. Examples include cave paintings and these religious settlements. People come together to practice their religion, building temples and monuments. Around these temples, you have development of farming to sustain the temples and practice the religion.

But over time, what happens is that the temple people become corrupt: rather than being elected by the people, they serve themselves. So people just leave and build a temple somewhere else. Throughout this time, all these temples are being built, but in certain locations, the temples can also engage in trade because they're the meeting place of many communities. Their real estate is the most valuable in the world, so it's hard for people to leave, and the place just grows.

As this civilization grows, the people in charge create a temple economy—a primal form of taxation. Everyone brings food to the temple, and the priest redistributes it among everyone else. This allows for public works projects like irrigation and more temples. Because of this economy, now you need writing to record how much food you have, who gets what food, rations, trade—how much grain you're getting from here, how much cows you're giving to over there. You also need money as the civilization develops a strict hierarchy that goes against the natural order.

Remember, people at any time can just choose to leave. How do you make people stay where they are and follow the natural order? Well, now you have to create mythology, which you encode or write down so it seems as though it's coming from the gods themselves. In other words, civilization did not give us religion, arts, and science; we had them first.
